job.system:
You are the AI assistant for the Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: The Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining (CADM) is a nonprofit advocacy organization based in Washington, DC. We believe that the industrial mining of the deep seabed, meaning the large-scale extraction of minerals from the ocean floor, poses a serious risk of irreversible destruction to deep-ocean ecosystems, and that no one currently knows how to conduct it without such damage. Our goal is a legally binding prohibition on commercial deep-sea mining, first in the United States and then through an international treaty. We work through lobbying, grassroots organizing, and public education.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which we strongly support. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
I'd read these as drafting problems for counsel to confirm, not legal conclusions. The ones most likely to let operations continue or to sink the bill are **#7, #12, #14, #24, #25, and #30**.

**Definitions and scope**

1. **§2(1)(A), per-vessel threshold.** The 10,000-ton limit applies to "a single vessel," with no aggregation rule for multiple vessels, sequential vessels, or affiliated companies. An operator can split output across several vessels, each under the line, and a 10,000-ton program is still meaningful pilot-scale extraction.

2. **§2(1)(A), "per year" and "metric tons."** The text doesn't say whether the year is calendar or rolling, whether weight is wet or dry, or who measures it. Because a violation only exists once the threshold is crossed, enforcers can't act against a vessel that is mining but hasn't yet exceeded it.

3. **§2(1)(A), "recovery," "seabed," and "other mineral resources."** None is defined. It is unclear whether the bill covers cobalt crusts, polymetallic sulfides, rare-earth muds, or subsoil, or whether "recovery" means lifting from the seafloor, bringing aboard, or delivery.

4. **§2(1)(A), 200-meter depth line.** Seabed mining at shallower depths, including parts of the continental shelf, falls outside the definition. The text also doesn't say how depth is measured or at what reference point.

5. **§2(1)(B), "the Secretary."** No Secretary is identified (Commerce, Interior, or another). An undefined official can't make the determination this clause depends on.

6. **§2(1)(B), the catch-all standard.** "Risks comparable to" subparagraph (A) has no criteria, process, deadline, or duty to act, and a violation carries criminal penalties under §5(b). That invites vagueness, fair-notice, and nondelegation challenges, and it gives a future administration a way to never use the clause.

7. **§2(2), "U.S. person."** The definition covers only citizens and corporations organized under State law. It leaves out permanent residents, LLCs, partnerships, trusts, and unincorporated associations. It also leaves out foreign subsidiaries of U.S. companies and entities organized in D.C. or the territories ("State" is undefined), so reincorporating or restructuring offshore avoids the prohibition.

8. **§2, missing definitions.** "Person," "United States," "State," "operator," "vessel," "exploration license," and "environmental assessment" are all used but undefined. Each gap is an opening for litigation over scope.

**Prohibition and exemptions**

9. **§3(a), "person in the United States."** Mining happens at sea, and "United States" is not defined to include the EEZ, the continental shelf, or the extended continental shelf. A non-U.S. person operating a foreign-flag vessel in U.S.-jurisdiction waters may not be covered.

10. **§3(a), "engage in."** The bill reaches only the mining itself. It does not cover financing, chartering, equipment supply, onshore processing, or purchase or import of minerals, and it creates no trade or port-state measures against foreign-mined material.

11. **§3, relationship to existing law.** The bill doesn't amend or repeal the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (30 U.S.C. ch. 26) or address OCSLA authority. It has no "notwithstanding any other provision of law" clause and doesn't bar agencies from issuing licenses or permits, so the conflict is left for courts and agencies to resolve. Please have counsel confirm the current status of those authorities.

12. **§3(b), grandfathering.** It doesn't say who must have issued the license (so a foreign or ISA-sponsored license could qualify). It has no expiration, and it doesn't bar renewal, expansion, or transfer. Whether "mining" can lawfully occur under an *exploration* license is unclear, and a rush to issue licenses before enactment is likely.

13. **§3(b), permits and pending applications.** Commercial recovery permits and pending applications aren't addressed. The silence invites takings and reliance claims, and because the bill has no compensation or transition provision, it is more exposed to challenge.

14. **§3(c), environmental assessment exemption.** It turns on the actor's stated "purpose," with no volume cap, duration limit, agency approval, independent oversight, or ban on retaining or selling recovered material. Test mining at industrial scale could be described as assessment.

**Registry**

15. **§4(a), covered vessels.** The 5,000-gross-ton threshold is unrelated to the 10,000-ton mining threshold, so smaller or temporarily outfitted vessels can mine above the threshold without registering. "Equipped for" and "operator" are undefined, there's no registration deadline, and it's unclear whether the duty reaches foreign operators.

16. **§4, no penalty.** §5 penalizes only violations of §3, so failing to register or report carries no stated consequence.

17. **§4(b), reporting.** The bill prescribes no content (location, tonnage, depth, mineral type), no verification or audit, no record retention, and no public access, and "certified by the operator" is the only check. It also sets no due date and doesn't address confidentiality claims under FOIA's trade-secret exemption.

18. **§4, implementing authority.** NOAA is given no rulemaking authority, no inspection authority, and no required vessel tracking (such as AIS), and no funds are authorized. The registry could be unworkable in practice.

**Penalties and enforcement**

19. **§5(a) vs. §8, timing conflict.** Penalties apply to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but the Act takes effect 180 days later. It's unclear whether conduct in the gap is penalized, and applying criminal penalties retroactively raises fair-notice problems.

20. **§5(a), civil penalty mechanics.** No agency is designated to assess penalties, and there's no administrative process, Attorney General civil action, injunctive relief, or forfeiture of vessels, equipment, or minerals. There's also no disgorgement, so for a large operation a $1,000,000 daily cap could be less than the profit.

21. **§5(b), "willfully."** Prosecutors would have to prove willfulness about technical elements like tonnage, depth, and the Secretary's determination. "Knowingly" is a lower, more provable bar, and the bill has no express liability for responsible corporate officers.

22. **§5, no citizen suit, whistleblower, or review provisions.** Enforcement depends entirely on executive-branch willingness. Nothing lets outside parties sue for violations or challenge failures to act.

23. **§3 and §5, no investigative authority.** The bill doesn't mention Coast Guard or NOAA boarding and inspection, subpoenas, or data-sharing. Monitoring distant at-sea activity depends on powers the bill never grants.

**International agreement**

24. **§6, hortatory and unenforceable.** The Secretary of State need only "seek to negotiate," and it's ambiguous whether the 18-month deadline modifies "seek" or "negotiate." There's no reporting requirement, no consequence for missing the deadline, no leverage such as trade measures, and "equivalent" prohibitions would import every loophole above.

**Duration, sunset, and effective date**

25. **§7(a) vs. §7(b), internal contradiction.** §7(a) keeps the prohibition until Congress finds mining can be done safely, but §7(b) ends the entire Act after 10 years regardless of any finding. The sunset overrides the science-based standard, and grandfathered license holders can simply wait it out.

26. **§7(a), joint resolution and standard.** A joint resolution must be presented to the President, so it is effectively a statute, and the text doesn't say whether it lifts the prohibition entirely or in part. "Serious harm" is undefined and is a weaker bar than "irreversible" harm, and the bill doesn't require, time, or fund the NASEM report or say who commissions it.

27. **§7(b), no savings clause.** Nothing preserves liability for violations that occurred before the sunset, and it's uncertain whether the general saving statute (1 U.S.C. 109) covers an expiring act. Counsel should confirm and add express language.

28. **§8, 180-day gap.** Operators can ramp up before the effective date. The bill has no interim moratorium on new licenses or permits and no wind-down rules for activity underway on day 181, and the 10-year sunset in §7(b) runs from enactment, not the effective date.

**General**

29. **No severability clause.** If a court struck a vulnerable provision such as §2(1)(B), the whole Act could be at risk.

30. **No anti-evasion provision.** The bill has no general rule treating restructuring, chartering, or reflagging done to avoid coverage as a violation. Combined with items 1, 7, and 9, that makes avoidance structurally easy.
